 US lifts nationwide ground stop, allowing flights to resume after hours of travel chaos
 The rare nationwide ground stop order, issued due to a communications problem affecting US air traffic control towers, caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest shutdown since the 9/11 attacks in 2001.
 A plane lands after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, US, November 13, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
 14 Nov 2026 09:40AM

 WASHINGTON: The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday (Nov 13) after a communications failure at air traffic control centres caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest nationwide shutdown since the Sep 11, 2001, attacks.
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened at 8.15pm Eastern Time (0115 GMT), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations.
 "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House.
 More than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already cancelled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days.

 Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country.
 The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by ageing technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.
 Traffic outside the terminal after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Dulles International Airport, in Dulles, Virginia, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Daniel Heuer
 Duane Hanson's "The Traveler" statue rests as people wait in Terminal B during a nationwide ground stop at Orlando International Airport in Orlando City, on Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Getty Images via AFP/Finn Gomez)
 Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36 pm when air traffic control centres experienced instability in radar and communications systems. Switches and routers carrying critical data became overloaded, producing inconsistent information and prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide, he said.
 "Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down," Duffy said, adding at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and were able to safely land thousands of planes.
 Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the ageing air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.
 United States Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy takes questions as US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin looks on in the James S Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington DC, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Elizabeth Frantz)
 US$50 BILLION AVIATION OVERHAUL
 Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for US$50 billion to modernise it.
 Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve US$30.1 billion to upgrade the nation's ageing airports and air traffic control infrastructure.
 "What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said.
 "Give us the money to fix it."
 A person waits during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Nov 13, 2026, in the Queens borough of New York City. (Photo: Getty Images via AFP/Adam Gray)
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was "zero evidence" so far that the outage resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, although investigators had not ruled out either possibility.
 "It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we're still looking," Mullin said.
 The National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation, he added.
 The outage appeared to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials. The network handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots. L3Harris did not respond to a request for comment.
 PAIN NOT OVER FOR PASSENGERS
 Though the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers was far from over. From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted and aircraft remained parked at gates.
 People wait inside a terminal at Dulles International Airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issues a national ground stop, in Dulles, Virginia, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Daniel Heuer)
 Thousands of passengers faced being stranded overnight. Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, had been scheduled to take a 9pm Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lome, Togo.
 Instead, he planned to spend the night at the airport before a rescheduled flight at 6am on Saturday.
 “I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.”
 Louise Maher, 47, was also caught up in the disruption at Newark after her British Airways flight to London was caught up in the aviation meltdown.
 “I might cry at some point but not yet,” she said.
 US airlines will not be required to provide compensation to stranded passengers because the carriers were not responsible for the FAA system failures.
 The only other nationwide ground stop since the Sep 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for about 90 minutes.
 Investors were already pricing in a financial hit to airlines. Shares of American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines fell between 1 per cent and 2 per cent in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about 3 per cent.
 American Airlines said it was prioritising flights to smaller cities outside its major hubs and international destinations to position aircraft and crews for a faster recovery.
